lead: Electronic stability program (ESP) is an active safety system that keeps a car pointing where the driver steers during a skid. It computes the yaw rate the steering and speed ask for, measures the yaw rate the car actually has, and brakes one wheel to create a correcting yaw moment. It also reduces engine torque when drive force is feeding the slide. You meet ESP in cars, SUVs and electric vehicles on wet roads, gravel and emergency swerves. Some syllabi call it ESC or VDC, for vehicle dynamics control.
prereq: You need: 5.4 for wheel slip and brake-pressure modulation, and Unit 3 for yaw rate and lateral acceleration sensors.

sections.h3: Desired yaw rate from the steering

blocks.text: Yaw rate r is how fast the car turns about a vertical axis through its centre of gravity, measured in rad/s. The driver asks for yaw by turning the steering wheel. At road-wheel steering angle δ rad and speed v m/s, a simple bicycle model gives a reference yaw rate. It is called a bicycle model because it lumps the two front wheels into one and the two rear wheels into one.

blocks.where: r<sub>des</sub> is the desired yaw rate in rad/s; v is vehicle speed in m/s; δ is road-wheel steering angle in rad; L is wheelbase in m; K is the understeer term in s²/m, so K v² is in m.

blocks.text: Large K means the car understeers more, so it needs more steering for the same yaw. ESP compares r<sub>des</sub> with the measured r<sub>meas</sub>. The error e = r<sub>des</sub> − r<sub>meas</sub> has a sign. Positive e means the car yaws less than asked, which is understeer. Negative e means it yaws more than asked, which is oversteer. The reference is also capped by tyre grip, so ESP never asks for a yaw rate that friction cannot support.

Five signals do most of the work. A yaw rate sensor, usually a small vibrating MEMS gyro, measures r. A lateral acceleration sensor measures sideways acceleration a<sub>y</sub> in m/s² and helps check grip and sensor plausibility. A steering angle sensor at the column measures δ. Four wheel-speed sensors, shared with ABS, give vehicle speed and wheel slip. A brake pressure sensor tells the hydraulic unit what pressure it has built.

The ESP hydraulic unit has a pump and solenoid valves. It can raise, hold or release brake pressure at one wheel while leaving the others alone. This is the same modulator family used by ABS and traction control. ABS stops wheel lock under braking; TCS stops drive-wheel spin; ESP adds yaw correction. ESP can also send a torque-reduction request to the engine or motor controller over CAN.
An off switch lets the driver disable ESP, for example to rock a car out of snow or run on a dynamometer. The switch does not add grip; it only stops automatic intervention.

In understeer the front tyres lose grip first. Actual yaw rate is lower than desired, so the nose runs wide. ESP brakes the rear inner wheel. That braking force acts behind the centre of gravity on the inside of the turn, and it creates a yaw moment that turns the nose into the corner. In the worked example the car is understeering, so the rear inner wheel is the correct choice.

In oversteer the rear tyres lose grip first. Actual yaw rate is higher than desired, so the rear slides out and the nose tucks in. ESP brakes the front outer wheel. That braking force acts ahead of the centre of gravity on the outside of the turn, and it creates an outward yaw moment that reduces the extra yaw. Braking the wrong wheel makes the skid worse, so this is the first thing an examiner tests.

Engine torque reduction backs up the brakes. On driven wheels, less torque means less wheelspin and more lateral grip left for steering. ESP cannot exceed tyre grip. On ice it can only help the car do what the tyres allow; it cannot create friction. It also cannot beat physics at high speed.

figure.caption: Steering angle sets a desired yaw rate; the compare block uses the measured yaw rate to find the error, and for this understeer case a rear-inner brake pulse adds yaw moment into the turn. The numbers are the worked example: desired 0.278 rad/s, measured 0.200 rad/s, error 0.078 rad/s.

spec.title: ESP yaw-rate correction
spec.aria: Steering angle builds a desired yaw rate, compared with the measured yaw rate; the difference drives braking of the rear inner wheel to create a correcting yaw moment.

examples.question: A car has wheelbase L = 2.6 m and understeer term K = 0.0025 s²/m. It travels at v = 20 m/s with road-wheel steering angle δ = 0.05 rad. The yaw rate sensor reads r<sub>meas</sub> = 0.200 rad/s. (a) Find the desired yaw rate in rad/s and °/s. (b) Find the yaw error. (c) State whether the car understeers or oversteers and which wheel ESP should brake.
steps: Error e = r<sub>des</sub> − r<sub>meas</sub> = 0.2778 − 0.200 = 0.0778 rad/s ≈ 0.078 rad/s = 4.456 °/s.
e is positive, so actual yaw is less than desired: understeer. Brake the rear inner wheel.
examples.answer: Desired yaw rate is 0.278 rad/s (15.915 °/s), measured is 0.200 rad/s (11.459 °/s), error is 0.078 rad/s (4.456 °/s); the car understeers, so ESP brakes the rear inner wheel.
examples.check:
import math
v = 20.0
delta = 0.05
L = 2.6
K = 0.0025
Kv2 = K * v * v
den = L + Kv2
r_des = v * delta / den
r_des_deg = r_des * 180.0 / math.pi
r_meas = 0.200
r_meas_deg = r_meas * 180.0 / math.pi
err = r_des - r_meas
err_deg = err * 180.0 / math.pi
print(f'{r_des:.3f}')
print(f'{r_des_deg:.3f}')
print(f'{r_meas:.3f}')
print(f'{r_meas_deg:.3f}')
print(f'{err:.3f}')
print(f'{err_deg:.3f}')

traps: Understeer is corrected by braking the rear inner wheel; oversteer is corrected by braking the front outer wheel. Reversing them is the classic wrong answer.
Use radians in r = vδ/(L + K v²). Convert degrees to rad first; °/s is only for display.
ESP cannot raise tyre grip. It only uses the grip available; a car on ice still slides.
ESP is not ABS or TCS. ABS stops wheel lock; TCS stops drive-wheel spin; ESP corrects yaw.
Positive error r<sub>des</sub> − r<sub>meas</sub> means understeer, not oversteer. Keep the sign.

quiz.q: What two yaw rates does ESP compare?
quiz.a: The desired yaw rate from steering angle and speed, and the measured yaw rate from the yaw rate sensor.

quiz.q: Why is the reference yaw rate capped by tyre grip?
quiz.a: So ESP does not demand a yaw rate that friction cannot support; it can correct only within the grip available.

quiz.q: A car has v = 15 m/s, δ = 0.04 rad, L = 2.5 m and K v² = 0.90 m. Compute the desired yaw rate in rad/s.
In a left turn, actual yaw rate is lower than desired. Which wheel should ESP brake, and why?
quiz.a: Understeer. Brake the rear inner wheel, the left rear. Its braking force behind the centre of gravity on the inside creates a yaw moment into the turn.

quiz.q: In a right turn, actual yaw rate is higher than desired. Which wheel should ESP brake?
quiz.a: Oversteer. Brake the front outer wheel, the front left. Its braking force ahead of the centre of gravity on the outside creates an outward yaw moment that reduces yaw.

quiz.q: Name three sensors used by ESP.
quiz.a: Any three of: yaw rate sensor, lateral acceleration sensor, steering angle sensor, wheel-speed sensors, brake pressure sensor.

quiz.q: What does the ESP off switch do, and what does it not do?
quiz.a: It disables automatic brake and torque interventions. It does not increase tyre grip or improve steering.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production ESP is now part of integrated chassis control: it shares a brake modulator with ABS, TCS, hill-hold and automated parking, and in electric cars it can use motor torque instead of brake pressure. Research looks at model-based yaw control, tyre-road friction estimation and sensor fusion with cameras and radar. Brake-by-wire and redundant sensors are needed for higher automation levels, see 5.8. Search terms: electronic stability control, yaw stability control, integrated chassis control, torque vectoring.
